data.title: Nitrianska Blatnica – a Great Moravian rotunda on Marhát
data.excerpt: In the forest zone of the Marhát massif at 450 m above sea level, 6 km east of the magnate's court at Ducové, stands the small Church of St George, known locally as Blatnický Ďurko. Excavation showed that its circular nave and horseshoe-shaped apse are identical in size to the rotunda at Ducové, that it formed part of an early medieval magnate's court, and that the mining hamlet beside it survived until the middle of the 13th century.
data.metaTitle: Nitrianska Blatnica – the rotunda of Blatnický Ďurko
data.metaDescription: The Church of St George on the Marhát massif has early medieval origins: a Great Moravian rotunda the size of the one at Ducové, and a place of pilgrimage.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: 6 km east of the magnate's court at Ducové, in the forest zone of the Marhát massif at 450 m above sea level, almost 5 km from Nitrianska Blatnica

keyFacts.label: The rotunda of Blatnický Ďurko
keyFacts.value: A circular nave with a horseshoe-shaped apse, internal diameter 730 cm, walls 73 cm thick — the same dimensions as the rotunda at Ducové

keyFacts.label: The court — earlier phase
keyFacts.value: An irregular quadrangular plan enclosed by palisades, covering about 9,000 m²

keyFacts.label: The court — later phase
keyFacts.value: Considerably smaller, about 3,500 m², evidently with an economic function (exploitation of a nearby iron-ore deposit)

keyFacts.label: Cemetery beside the rotunda
keyFacts.value: More than 120 graves from the 11th to the mid-13th century; male skeletons clearly predominate — evidence of a mining population

keyFacts.label: Iron-ore extraction
keyFacts.value: A series of prospecting pits and mining hollows in the forest zone of the Nitrianska Blatnica and Vozokany cadastral areas; the largest up to 20 m across, about 8 m deep

keyFacts.label: Excavator
keyFacts.value: The site was investigated by Alexander Ruttkay — the same man who excavated Kostolec (Ducové)

keyFacts.label: Today
keyFacts.value: A traditional place of pilgrimage; Mass is still celebrated in the church on St George's day

timeline.title: The earlier court is founded
timeline.description: The earlier magnate's court near Nitrianska Blatnica was founded in the 9th century, partly contemporary with the court at Ducové.

timeline.title: The rotunda of Blatnický Ďurko is built
timeline.description: A rotunda with the same dimensions as the church at Ducové (internal diameter 730 cm, walls 73 cm thick) — both laid out with the Lombard foot (36.5 cm), as was the double-apsed rotunda at Mikulčice.

timeline.title: The later, smaller court is founded
timeline.description: A second court covering about 3,500 m² (as against 9,000 m² in the earlier phase), evidently with an economic function connected with the extraction of iron ore.

timeline.title: The later court ends and a small hamlet appears
timeline.description: After the demise of the court a small hamlet came into being here, with log-built dwellings, outdoor ovens and tar-production pits; a churchyard cemetery grew up around the rotunda.

timeline.title: A charter of King Béla III
timeline.description: It mentions Stojislav, whose mother the king granted the lifelong use of estates called Sárfew (Blatnica) as a reward for her son's heroism in battle.

timeline.title: The hamlet and the function of the rotunda come to an end
timeline.description: The original function of the rotunda also ceased; at roughly the same time several other hamlets in the surroundings were abandoned and their fields became overgrown with forest.

timeline.title: Anna Thurzová restores the church
timeline.description: The church was rebuilt from its ruins by Anna Thurzová in memory of her husband František, who fell at Mohács.

timeline.title: Archaeological excavation
timeline.description: Field inspections and excavation confirmed that the Church of St George was built as early as the Early Middle Ages, with dimensions identical to those of the rotunda at Ducové.

children.text: At a distance of 6 km to the east of the magnate's court at Ducové, already on the Nitra-region side of the Marhát massif, in the forest zone at an elevation of 450 m above sea level and almost 5 km from Nitrianska Blatnica, stands the small Church of St George, a traditional place of pilgrimage for the inhabitants of the neighbouring parts of the Váh and Nitra regions.
According to the written sources on which the older literature relies, the church was rebuilt from its ruins in 1530 by Anna Thurzová in memory of her husband František, who fell at Mohács.

Field inspections and the subsequent archaeological excavation carried out here in 1974 and in 1976–1980 showed that the Church of St George was built as early as the Early Middle Ages, and that the thickness of its walls, its circular nave and its horseshoe-shaped apse are in their dimensions entirely identical with the rotunda at Ducové. The church, known locally as Jurko, had two medieval phases — pre-Romanesque and Romanesque. Around 1530 the repair mentioned in the charters took place here, together with the Renaissance vaulting of the ancient building, which had long been in ruins. The present appearance of the church, with its tower and the so-called hermitage, corresponds to the rebuilding carried out in the middle of the 17th century. Thanks to these alterations the church as such has survived to the present day, but its appearance, especially as regards the upper part, differs substantially from the original Great Moravian building. These alterations and its present appearance therefore do not evoke such a sense of antiquity as does the Church of St Margaret at Kopčany. Despite the later alterations, however, it is still an originally Great Moravian church.

children.text: Pavel Dvořák, in his book Stopy dávnej minulosti 3 (Traces of the Distant Past 3), states that "the little Church of St George has foundations — accurate to the centimetre — of exactly the same size as the Great Moravian church at Ducové, only seven kilometres away along the road between the mountain ridges. Ďurko and Kostolec therefore lie on the road that linked Mikulčice and Nitra. It was fortunate that both Kostolec and Nitrianska Blatnica had the same excavator, Alexander Ruttkay, for it is hard to say whether anyone else would have noticed that the internal diameters of the two rotundas (730 centimetres) and the thickness of their walls (73 centimetres) are identical. All the dimensions are derived from a basic unit of length — 36.5 centimetres, the so-called Lombard foot (the two rotundas also agree in their structural dimensions, measuring over 12.2 metres on the outside and almost 11 metres on the inside). The same unit was used to lay out another Great Moravian church, the double-apsed rotunda at Mikulčice. In 1975 the surroundings and the architecture of the chapel began to be uncovered. It turned out that the oldest part of the building could be reliably recognised within the old walls: the circular rotunda and the horseshoe-shaped apse. It had unusually shallow foundations, 20–30 cm deep, but in places resting on the rock bedrock. The original walls of flat stones bonded with mortar survived to a height of about a metre. The added masonry, separated by a clearly visible break, looked quite different." Blatnický Ďurko was evidently built at the same time as the rotunda at Ducové or the double-apsed rotunda at Mikulčice. All three buildings belong to the time of Svatopluk and have identical dimensions.

children.text: In his paper VÝZNAMNÉ ARCHEOLOGICKÉ LOKALITY Z VČASNÉHO STREDOVEKU V OBLASTI POVAŽSKÉHO INOVCA (Important early medieval sites in the Považský Inovec region), Alexander Ruttkay states that "according to the results of the archaeological excavation, the rotunda of St George formed part of an early medieval magnate's court. It was, however, situated within a separate residence on a small promontory above the court's own enclosure. Of the presumed residence beside the rotunda, in ground disturbed by the construction of the school, converted in the 19th century into a forester's lodge, only a fragment of a feature cut into the rock bedrock was recorded, and sherds of 9th–10th-century pottery were found there. In the small cemetery beside the rotunda there were also bones from disturbed graves predating the 11th century, and near the entrance on the western side of the nave a large key belonging to the early medieval phase of the rotunda was found, for example.

was situated below the promontory with the rotunda, on the plateau known as Púšť. The excavation was able to focus on only a small part of the area of the court. It can be stated, however, that in the investigated parts of the meadow, below which a small stream once flowed, most of the ground-level features had been destroyed in the past by ploughing. The extent and the chronological relationships of the court could be traced mainly from the course of the palisade trenches cut into the rock bedrock, while the settlement layout with its ground-level dwellings was indicated only by stones from ovens and by sherd material. The court has two chronological phases. In both cases it is an irregular quadrangular plan of an area enclosed by palisades. The earlier phase covered about 9,000 m², the later one was considerably smaller, about 3,500 m². Unlike the court at Ducové, this one may have had a particularly pronounced economic function, evidently connected with the exploitation of a nearby deposit of iron ore. Insights into both phases of the court and into their links with the routes from the Nitra region to the Váh region can be extended above all by excavation on the southern side of the Púšť meadow, which adjoins the road to the Gajda Pass (602 m a.s.l.) south of Marhát.

children.text: The development at Nitrianska Blatnica is reflected in the identification of two non-contemporary courts. The earlier court was founded as early as the 9th century. It was thus partly contemporary with the court at Ducové. The second (smaller) court is later and belongs to the 10th–11th century. In the course of the 11th century, after the demise of the later court, a small hamlet came into being here. The features associated with it could be recognised only in a hollow in the terrain near the former stream. Traces of ground-level dwellings, probably of log construction, outdoor ovens and tar-production pits were recorded. The rotunda, probably already damaged before that, underwent a Romanesque rebuilding. From the 11th century to the middle of the 13th century a churchyard cemetery lay around it, and it was excavated in full. Among the more than 120 graves, which indicate a small buried population, the skeletons of men clearly predominate. This gender asymmetry of the population is quite unusual and points to a distinctive way of life." The founding, the life and the demise of the small hamlet were evidently connected with the source of iron ore, and the presence of miners explains the small number of women's graves beside the chapel: extracting ore was men's work. It was geologists who first pointed to the ancient extraction of ore on the eastern slopes of Marhát. In the field, in the forest zone within the cadastral areas of the villages of Nitrianska Blatnica and Vozokany, a whole series of hollows and mounds was recorded which can be regarded as prospecting pits and mining hollows. Probably the largest of them is up to 20 m in diameter and about 8 m deep.

children.text: Ruttkay goes on: "The demise of the hamlet and of the original function of the rotunda came about no later than around the middle of the 13th century. At roughly that period several other hamlets were also abandoned and the partly cultivated land became overgrown with forest. This is attested by the surviving field systems and sunken trackways in the forest zone and by a whole series of probable names of these hamlets in the 14th- and 15th-century boundary surveys of Radošina and Nitrianska Blatnica. They include, for example, the names Prylecz, Prynyoa, Dehchyche, Lwsne, Grechyk and Stopparcz."

Dvořák writes something interesting in connection with the church and its surroundings: "There is one piece of information in a charter of King Béla III of 1185 which is admittedly less reliable, but all the more interesting for that, because it mentions a certain Stojislav who suffered such severe wounds in battle that after his death the king granted Stojislav's mother, as a reward for her son's heroism, the lifelong use of her son's extensive estates. This was not common practice; estates were not granted to women, they were received as a reward by warriors, and if there was no male descendant they reverted to the king. It is hard to say what exactly led Béla III to take such an unusual step, but it is important that the estates in question were called Sárfew, that is Blatnica, and that Stojislav is a Slavic name. It really is an unusual situation if a nobleman of Blatnica with a Slavic name lays down his life for the king two centuries after the fall of Great Moravia and the king shows his gratitude in such a way. It is hard to say whether this is a coincidence or a piece of remarkable history. Written records are few; popular tradition, by contrast, is very much alive. On St George's day Mass is still celebrated in the church even today, the church has been a place of pilgrimage from time immemorial, in the inter-war republic fairs were held here and in 1935, for example, as many as forty thousand pilgrims are said to have come. Something long forgotten once stood at this place; tradition merely reminds us that this is no ordinary church, but it could make nothing of it."
